question.knowledge_point: Finding a Particular Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE With Polynomial Forcing
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y={x}^{2}-2.
$$

Find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
question.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma $ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
2(2\alpha x+\beta )+2(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )={x}^{2}-2
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
2\alpha {x}^{2}+(4\alpha +2\beta )x+(2\beta +2\gamma )={x}^{2}-2.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2\alpha =1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 4\alpha +2\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\beta +2\gamma =-2\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{1}{2},\beta =-1,\gamma =0.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-x.
$$
